title: Mesa 3: Agent-based modeling with Python in 2025

key_points.claim: Mesa is an open-source Python ABM framework (v3.1.5). It is a tooling and infrastructure paper, not a substantive artificial-society model.
key_points.evidence_quote: Mesa is an open-source Python framework for agent-based modeling (ABM) that enables researchers to create, analyze, and visualize agent-based simulations.

key_points.claim: ABM's conceptual basis is heterogeneous autonomous agents whose local interactions produce emergent aggregate dynamics. It cites Epstein & Axtell's Growing Artificial Societies as foundational.
key_points.evidence_quote: Agent-based models (ABMs) are composed of autonomous, heterogeneous agents interacting locally with other agents. These interactions give rise to emergent phenomena.

key_points.claim: The paper places Mesa in the history of ABM tooling. NetLogo (1999) is accessible but limited to small models. MASON (2003) is faster but hard for non-programmers. Mesa was built to serve web hosting and the Python ecosystem.
key_points.evidence_quote: NetLogo is the most widely adopted tool and the first to make ABMs accessible, but it only allows for small models. MASON is Java-based, allowing for advancements in scalability and speed above NetLogo

key_points.claim: Application domains cited: infrastructure resilience, energy auctions, transport, recommender systems, climate adaptation (household behaviour), COVID SEIR, and edge computing. Mesa has been cited in more than 500 papers.
key_points.evidence_quote: Mesa has been applied to modeling a wide range of phenomena from economics and sociology to ecology and epidemiology and has been cited in more than 500 papers and 800 authors.

key_points.claim: Agents aspect: Mesa 3 adds an AgentSet class for filtering, grouping and aggregating agents, and drops the fixed Scheduler API. Activation is now flexible: sequential, random, multi-stage or per type.
key_points.evidence_quote: the newly added AgentSet class provides a more flexible way to activate agents. These changes include the removal of the Scheduler API and its previously available fixed patterns.

key_points.claim: Space aspect: Mesa 3 supports discrete spaces (orthogonal Moore and von Neumann grids, hex grids, network, Voronoi mesh) and continuous space. It has specialised agent classes (FixedAgent, CellAgent, Grid2DMovingAgent) and numpy-based PropertyLayers for cell-level environment properties.
key_points.evidence_quote: Mesa 3 provides both discrete (cell-based) and continuous space implementations.

key_points.claim: Time aspect: tick-based stepping is the default. Experimental next-event scheduling (DiscreteEventSimulator) and hybrid tick/event modes are also offered.
key_points.evidence_quote: Mesa also includes experimental support for next-event time progression through the DiscreteEventSimulator.

key_points.claim: Experimentation aspect: reproducibility comes from seeded random number generators. There is a DataCollector with model, agent and agent-type reporters, pandas integration, and batch parameter sweeps.
key_points.evidence_quote: Since ABMs are typically stochastic simulations, Mesa includes a random number generator and, for reproducibility purposes, allows the user to pass a seed.

key_points.claim: Visualization and ecosystem: SolaraViz gives interactive browser-based exploration. Extensions include Mesa-Geo for geospatial modeling and Mesa-Frames for high-performance simulation. Development involves 7 maintainers and over 140 contributors.
key_points.evidence_quote: Mesa's visualization module, SolaraViz, allows for interactive browser-based model exploration.

reliability_notes: Full text fetched (a 6-page peer-reviewed JOSS software paper, CC BY 4.0). It describes a framework, not empirical findings or societal model results, so it is useful for the tooling, infrastructure and architecture parts of a state-of-the-art summary. It has little on social-mechanism content such as norms, institutions, cognition or economies. The authors are the Mesa maintainers, so the claims are self-descriptive, and comparisons with NetLogo and MASON are brief and unbenchmarked.
